title: Type 2 Diabetes Surging Among Young Women as Obesity Epidemic Shifts Younger
excerpt: An Imperial College London study finds a 'clear generational divide' in diabetes diagnoses, with women aged 20 to 39 facing the steepest rise in cases while rates decline among older adults.
body:
A Generational Divide in Diabetes

Type 2 diabetes is rapidly becoming a disease of the young, with women in their twenties and thirties bearing the heaviest burden, according to a major new study from Imperial College London.

The research, published in Lancet Regional Health Europe, examined type 2 diabetes trends across England between 2011 and 2024. It found a stark "generational divide": diagnoses are rising sharply among adults under 40, even as they decline by roughly 2% per year among those aged 60 to 79.

The steepest trajectory belongs to women aged 20 to 39, where new diagnoses are climbing at 3% annually. Separate Diabetes UK data shows type 2 diagnoses in women under 40 surged 47% between 2017/18 and 2023/24 — compared with 34% for men in the same age group and 22% for women aged 40 to 79.

Obesity Pulling the Age of Diagnosis Down

The Imperial team identified rising obesity as the engine behind the shift. Over the study period, average BMI at diagnosis rose twice as quickly among younger adults as among older ones.

"The earlier onset of severe obesity in young people is increasing their type 2 diabetes risk in early life and pulling down their age at diagnosis," said Dr Shivani Misra, the study's lead author. She noted that while previous research focused on higher susceptibility among ethnic minority groups, the new study showed rates were "increasing in white populations too."

"We have known for a long time that obesity is linked to type 2 diabetes, but what is new from this study is the scale of the change occurring in younger adults."

— Dr Shivani Misra, Imperial College London

The UK has 4.7 million people with a diabetes diagnosis, about 90% of them type 2. Misra said young people appeared "particularly vulnerable to today's obesogenic environment," and the study's authors recommended targeting younger populations with preventative interventions including weight-loss medications.

The Gestational Diabetes Gap

Diabetes UK has flagged poor follow-up care for gestational diabetes as another contributor. The condition affects 10% to 20% of pregnant women and typically resolves after birth, but significantly raises long-term type 2 risk.

The first national gestational diabetes audit from NHS England found only 57% of affected women received the recommended annual HbA1c test, and just 4.5% were referred to the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme. Within a decade, 15% of women with gestational diabetes progressed to type 2.

A Sharper Edge for South Asians

The findings carry particular weight for the Indian diaspora. South Asians develop type 2 diabetes nearly two decades earlier than Western populations, driven by a combination of the "thin-fat phenotype" — lower BMI but higher body fat and insulin resistance — and rapid dietary shifts accompanying urbanisation.

"Within a decade, 15% of women with gestational diabetes progressed to type 2.</p> <blockquote class="pull-quote"> <p>"Pregnancy shouldn't be a pathway to ill health."

A January 2026 study from Max Healthcare in New Delhi warned that India's standard diabetes risk tools underestimate the threat to younger individuals by weighting age too heavily. Research from the Indian Council for Medical Research shows an Indian woman aged 20 in a metropolitan area faces a 64.6% lifetime risk of developing diabetes. India's prediabetes-to-diabetes progression rate of 14% to 18% per year dwarfs the 2.5% rate in the United States.

What Comes Next

Early-onset type 2 diabetes is more aggressive than the later-onset form, leading to faster deterioration in blood sugar control and earlier complications including heart disease and kidney failure. Diabetes UK is pushing for prevention strategies that account for shifting demographics, rather than treating type 2 as primarily a condition of middle and old age.

For the Indian diaspora, the message is direct: screening and lifestyle intervention should begin earlier, particularly for women with a family history of diabetes or a history of gestational diabetes.
